stories.topic: The Poisoned Apple Almost Ended Oppenheimer Before He Began
stories.summary: At Cambridge, Oppenheimer was forced to do experimental physics, work that bored and crushed him. He told a friend, 'The lab work is a terrible bore and it is impossible to feel that I am learning anything.' His misery was so acute that he left a poisoned apple on his physics tutor's desk. The university opened an inquiry; only because his parents were wealthy did he avoid expulsion (on condition he undergo psychiatric treatment). When he subsequently moved to Gottingen, the world's great temple of theoretical physics in the 1920s, with classmates like Dirac and von Neumann under Max Born, he flourished.
stories.insight: Genius is not just about innate talent — it requires environmental fit. A standardized one-size-fits-all system can throttle the very minds it should be unlocking. The tragedy of Oppenheimer 'is not the Oppenheimer who was, but the many, many countless Oppenheimers who never even were' because the system never gave them their Gottingen.

stories.topic: Leo Szilard's Aha Moment Crossing a London Street
stories.summary: Leo Szilard was crossing a road in London with his mind lost in physics. As he walked across, the idea struck him — neutrons could trigger a chain reaction in uranium atoms. That single moment connected twenty-to-thirty years of accumulated physics into an engineering project: you could shatter atoms of uranium and turn it into either explosive energy or controlled energy. Terrified that Hitler might get there first, Szilard reached Einstein, who wrote the famous letter to Roosevelt, and the Manhattan Project was born.
stories.insight: Big ideas often arrive in mundane moments — but only after decades of preparation have laid the substrate. Until Szilard's epiphany, E = mc² had been a curiosity for thirty years; the engineering pathway simply did not exist. Insight is what happens when accumulated understanding suddenly clicks into a usable shape.

stories.topic: Niels Bohr Said It Was Impossible — They Did It Anyway
stories.summary: When Niels Bohr was finally let in on the Manhattan Project, his initial reaction was: 'It's impossible, it can't be done. You'll have to turn the entire United States into a factory.' Then he later said, 'And you guys did.' The world's biggest factory ever built was constructed for uranium enrichment, and an even bigger one for plutonium processing. A team of a few thousand people, led by a 38-year-old Oppenheimer, took it through to the finish line.
stories.insight: Even one of the greatest minds of the century could not see the path to the goal until it had been walked. Sometimes the impossible only looks impossible until the right person, with the right team, in the right environment, simply refuses to accept it.

stories.topic: Oppenheimer Studied Sanskrit and Quoted the Gita at Trinity
stories.summary: Oppenheimer was bohemian, intellectually restless, with a Republican-supporter past from the 1936 Spanish Civil War, a brother in the Communist Party, and an eclectic wife. As one expression of that range, he learned Sanskrit — Ajay challenges Indians to imagine themselves learning Aramaic for comparison. At the moment of the first atomic bomb test in July 1945, Oppenheimer remembered lines from the Gita where Vishnu shows his Vishwarup form to Arjun: 'I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.'
stories.insight: True genius combines technical mastery with humanistic depth. Knowing how the bomb worked was necessary but not sufficient — Oppenheimer also brought the moral and metaphorical vocabulary to understand what he had done. Specialists know what; Renaissance figures also know what it means.

stories.topic: Truman, the Hydrogen Bomb, and the Bureaucratic Knives
stories.summary: When Oppenheimer told President Truman, 'I think I have blood on my hands' for Hiroshima and Nagasaki, Truman bristled — 'I'm the president, I decided, who are you?' Then on the hydrogen bomb, where Edward Teller was driven by pure scientific curiosity (could nuclear fission ignite a fusion reaction?), Oppenheimer began to ask: do you really want to build something 100x more destructive than a bomb that can already destroy a city? In doing so, he 'accumulated the anger and hatred of a whole bunch of bureaucrats.' All of this fed straight into the McCarthyite trial that destroyed his public career.
stories.insight: Bureaucracies dislike articulate, charismatic, knowledgeable figures. Oppenheimer had the curse of walking into rooms knowing more than anyone, and the gift of saying things in a sweet elegant fashion that persuaded people. To gray, bloodless powerful people on the losing side of arguments, that is unforgivable.

stories.topic: The Rehabilitation: A Country That Admitted Its Mistake
stories.summary: About two years before this episode, after activists used Freedom of Information access to dig into the rigged 1954 hearings — the illegal evidence-gathering, the rule-of-law violations, the character assassination — the U.S. government formally retracted the verdict and reinstated Oppenheimer's security clearance, decades after his death. The Department of Energy issued an official order. The descendants of the persecutors and the persecuted were both involved in surfacing the story.
stories.insight: States are cruel coercive creatures and make mistakes all the time — but a first-world country is one where independent citizens can write letters, challenge the government, and force it to publicly admit error. Ajay's painful contrast: in India, we don't even expect the state to try.

stories.topic: Roy Cohn — From McCarthy to Trump
stories.summary: The chief counsel who worked for Senator Joe McCarthy and tried to subpoena Oppenheimer in the 1950s was Roy Cohn. Roy Cohn would later become the mentor, teacher, philosopher, and guide of Donald J. Trump. The same nationalist, power-hungry, unethical culture that crucified Oppenheimer runs as a continuous thread through American politics across generations.
stories.insight: Cultures of cruelty don't die with their first generation; they get passed down by personal mentorship. Sometimes when we are told 'there are very fine people on both sides,' history's distance reveals it was never a fair fight — the same archetype was on the wrong side then and is on the wrong side now.

stories.topic: Madhu's Patience and Arrival in Bangalore
stories.summary: Amit went with their mutual friend Madhu Menon to see Denis Villeneuve's Arrival in a Bangalore theatre. Fifteen minutes in, Madhu was complaining: 'This is so slow, what is happening?' Amit, by contrast, was loving every minute of it — astonished that a mainstream studio film could carry that level of integrity and thought.
stories.insight: A small affectionate moment about how taste diverges between friends — and a reminder that the patience required for serious art is itself a learned, even minority, skill in an attention-economy culture.

stories.topic: Tim de Lisle: 'When in Doubt, Play Your Shots'
stories.summary: When Amit joined Wisden in 2001 as a young writer, his editor's editor was Tim de Lisle (later editor of Wisden Almanac and The Economist's Intelligent Life). Tim's writing tips were largely about clarity, but one tenet stayed with Amit: 'When in doubt, play your shots.' Amit was a terrible writer in those days — exuberant, flamboyant, showing off — but the maxim said: don't restrain yourself artificially when bursting with the passion to create. Restraint comes naturally with maturity.
stories.insight: Creative growth requires permission to overreach. You learn what not to do by trying everything; you cannot edit what you have not first written. The same logic applies more broadly than writing — to filmmaking (Nolan), to research, to ambition itself.

stories.topic: The Power Broker — Caro, Moses, and a Lost 200,000 Words on Jane Jacobs
stories.summary: Robert Caro told a publisher he'd take a few months to write a biography of Robert Moses. Twelve or thirteen years later, he produced a million-word book that had to be cut to 800,000 — at the publisher's insistence that a paperback couldn't be longer or split into two volumes. The cut included a book-length section (around 200,000 words) on Jane Jacobs by 'one of the greatest biographers who has ever lived.' Caro then began a Lyndon Johnson biography in the late 70s; one volume remains, and he took longer to write about LBJ's Senate years than LBJ spent in the Senate.
stories.insight: Form constraints can destroy intellectual treasures — that lost Jane Jacobs section now exists nowhere. The internet age dissolves those constraints (an author today could simply post the rest), but it arrived too late for The Power Broker. Borges' map-as-large-as-the-world idea applies: total fidelity is impossible, but the pursuit produces masterpieces.

recommendations.item: The Making of the Atomic Bomb
recommendations.creator: Richard Rhodes
recommendations.context: Rhodes' 1986 history of the Manhattan Project, considered the definitive book on the subject — Hans Bethe is said to have remarked that nobody could tell this story.
recommendations.reason: Ajay's number-one recommendation on Oppenheimer. The early-20th-century physics community took Rhodes on as their 'poet laureate,' giving him the access and trust to tell their story — and he carries the lay reader along while explaining complex science. Even readers who think they aren't 'science people' should read it, because all great acts of creation are, finally, human projects.

recommendations.creator: Robert Jungk
recommendations.context: The 1956 biographical history of Oppenheimer and the atomic age — Ajay first read it at age twelve.
recommendations.reason: The book that planted Oppenheimer in Ajay's imagination as a child and that he returned to many times. Foundational for any reader who wants to understand the Manhattan Project from the biographical side, before Rhodes existed.

recommendations.item: The Power Broker: Robert Moses and the Fall of New York
recommendations.creator: Robert Caro
recommendations.context: Caro's Pulitzer-winning 800,000-word biography of New York's master bureaucrat Robert Moses.
recommendations.reason: A masterpiece working on three levels at once: a biography of Moses the man, a biography of New York City as it was reshaped by his top-down vision, and a study of how power corrupts and corrodes the soul. 'It is not just about Moses, it is not just about New York, it is not just about power. It's about all of us. Everything is everything.'

recommendations.item: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
recommendations.creator: Jane Jacobs
recommendations.context: Jacobs' foundational work on cities and urban planning, arguing for organic growth over top-down imposition.
recommendations.reason: One of Amit's intellectual heroes. Jacobs argued that cities are about people, not buildings, and coined 'the ballet of the streets.' A vital antidote to Indian middle-class instincts that yearn for an authoritarian planner; modern urban thinking remains rare and precious in India and this is a 'fundamental input into our brains for what can go right and what can go wrong.'

recommendations.creator: Christopher Nolan
recommendations.context: Nolan's then-unreleased biographical film about J. Robert Oppenheimer.
recommendations.reason: Amit hadn't yet seen it but framed Nolan as an 'author at scale' — bringing the sensibility of an artistic, intimate-drama filmmaker to massive cinematic experiences. Nolan switched studios from Warner Brothers to Universal because Warner planned a same-day HBO Max release and Nolan is a stickler for the big-screen experience.

recommendations.creator: Christopher Nolan
recommendations.context: Nolan's 2017 WWII evacuation film.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'one of the greatest war films I've ever seen.' Ajay independently invokes it as evidence Nolan can handle history he cares deeply about — which is part of why Ajay both wants and dreads what Nolan will do with Oppenheimer.

recommendations.creator: Denis Villeneuve
recommendations.context: Villeneuve's first big-studio film — a science fiction film about first contact.
recommendations.reason: An example of what Amit calls a golden age of mainstream cinema — a director keeping his identity and bringing intellectual concepts onto the big-budget screen. The film that hooked Amit on Villeneuve.

recommendations.creator: Denis Villeneuve
recommendations.context: Villeneuve's 2017 sequel to Ridley Scott's Blade Runner.
recommendations.reason: Amit thinks the sequel is better than the original — 'which is saying a lot, because the original is a masterpiece.' Another data point that mainstream Hollywood is still capable of giving great filmmakers room.

recommendations.creator: Ridley Scott
recommendations.context: Ridley Scott's 1982 original.
recommendations.reason: Acknowledged as a masterpiece, and Scott himself was one of Christopher Nolan's inspirations — closing the loop between the auteurs Amit admires in mainstream cinema.

recommendations.creator: Tim de Lisle
recommendations.context: The writing book by Amit's first editor's editor at Wisden, later editor of Wisden Almanac and Intelligent Life.
recommendations.reason: Tim's tenets are about clarity, and Amit uses some of his examples in his own writing course. The book is the source of the dictum that shaped young Amit: 'When in doubt, play your shots.'

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's online writing course.
recommendations.reason: Self-recommendation, and the place he passes on lessons from teachers like Tim de Lisle to a new generation of writers.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's 2008 column on the Indian education system.
recommendations.reason: The piece that crystallised his argument that education is the great market failure of our age. In supermarkets you get 40 flavors of potato chips because markets respect individual difference; in education we use a one-size-fits-all 19th-century industrial model that asks the fish to climb a tree.

recommendations.item: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with the economist Karthik Muralidharan on Indian education.
recommendations.reason: Source of the piercing observation Amit returns to here: the Indian education system is optimized for sorting, not teaching. It just sorts the already-bright minds into IITs and IIMs and lets us mistake selection for instruction.

recommendations.item: A Deep Dive Into Ukraine vs Russia (Episode 335, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's earlier conversation on the Ukraine-Russia war.
recommendations.reason: Ajay invokes it as a parallel to the Manhattan Project: in extraordinary times, organizations are forced to recruit mavericks. The Ukrainian side built an 'Uber for artillery' precisely because survival pressure broke the normal bureaucratic instinct to suppress unconventional thinkers.

recommendations.item: The Poetic Feminism of Paromita Vohra (Episode 339, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Paromita Vohra
recommendations.context: Amit's then-latest Seen and the Unseen episode, with the filmmaker and writer Paromita Vohra.
recommendations.reason: Vohra makes the same argument as the Oppenheimer story: organizations everywhere optimize for the mean — for mediocrity — and crush anyone who thinks differently. The convergence of two very different conversations on the same diagnosis is itself the point.

recommendations.item: Jahnavi and the Cyclotron (Episode 319, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Jahnavi Phalkey
recommendations.context: Amit's episode with the historian of science Jahnavi Phalkey.
recommendations.reason: The Indian counterpart to the Oppenheimer story — three scientists in 1940s India contesting how to set up theoretical and nuclear physics institutions. One won, two lost; once the extraordinary moment ended, normal politics took over.

recommendations.creator: Jahnavi Phalkey
recommendations.context: Phalkey's history of nuclear physics in 20th-century India.
recommendations.reason: The book version of the Indian parallel to Oppenheimer — how Homi Bhabha, Vikram Sarabhai, and Meghnad Saha contested the early architecture of Indian science, with all the politics that follows from extraordinary people in extraordinary times.

recommendations.creator: Isaiah Berlin
recommendations.context: Berlin's classic essay distinguishing thinkers who know one big thing (hedgehogs) from those who know many things (foxes).
recommendations.reason: Invoked as the lens for Oppenheimer the Renaissance man — who is, unusually, both a fox in his range of interests and a hedgehog in his depth as a theoretical physicist.

recommendations.creator: Paul Graham
recommendations.context: Graham's framework on aggressively-conventional vs. aggressively-independent minds.
recommendations.reason: Carry-over from Episode 1. Used to frame Oppenheimer's persecutors as the aggressively conventional-minded, and thinkers like Rutherford and pre-conversion Einstein as conventional-minded skeptics who declared atomic energy 'moonshine' before the engineering was visible.

recommendations.creator: Kai Bird
recommendations.context: Bird's New Yorker piece on the U.S. government's 2022 reversal of the Oppenheimer security-clearance decision.
recommendations.reason: The reference for the rehabilitation story Ajay tells. Required reading on how, decades after the fact, citizen-led archival work and FOI access can force a state to admit error in writing.

recommendations.item: The enduring legacy of Leo Szilard
recommendations.creator: Ashutosh Jogalekar
recommendations.context: A blog essay about Szilard from Field of Science.
recommendations.reason: Backs up the chain-reaction-on-a-London-street story and Szilard's pivotal but underappreciated role in initiating the bomb project — including writing the letter that Einstein then signed and sent to Roosevelt.

recommendations.creator: Jorge Luis Borges
recommendations.context: Borges' one-paragraph fiction about an empire whose cartographers made a map the same size as the territory.
recommendations.reason: Invoked to capture the paradox of Caro's biographical method — total fidelity demands more space than the world contains, and is out of date the next instant. A meditation on the trade-off between completeness and usability.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's Substack piece arguing that internet-era publishing dissolves the old length and form constraints of paper.
recommendations.reason: Connects to the lost 200,000 words on Jane Jacobs in The Power Broker. Today, an author could simply put the remainder online; the constraint that destroyed that text no longer exists.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy.
recommendations.reason: Listed in the show notes as a foundational text behind Ajay's worldview on state, criticism, and bureaucratic instincts toward articulate critics like Oppenheimer.

core_ideas.explanation: Oppenheimer had the curse of walking into rooms knowing more than anyone there, and the gift of saying things in a sweet, elegant fashion that persuaded people. Bureaucracies cannot tolerate that combination — articulate, charismatic, knowledgeable figures threaten the gray, bloodless powerful people on the losing side of arguments. The same trait that makes a person necessary in extraordinary times makes them intolerable in normal times.
core_ideas.quote: Normal governments and bureaucratic formations have a way of disliking the articulate, charismatic, knowledgeable figure.

core_ideas.explanation: The modern education system was designed in the 19th century to churn out workers for the industrial revolution: same-age cohorts, same subjects, identical tests, rote learning. In India taken to its extreme. What it actually does, as Karthik Muralidharan argued on Amit's podcast, is sort the already-bright minds (into IITs and IIMs) — not teach. Markets give us 40 flavors of potato chips because they respect individual difference; education gives every fish the same tree to climb.
core_ideas.quote: If you're going to teach a monkey to climb a tree, you're testing the fish on how well the fish can climb the tree, which makes absolutely no sense.

core_ideas.concept: The Tragedy is the Oppenheimers Who Never Were
core_ideas.explanation: Oppenheimer himself almost wasted away in Cambridge; only the move to Gottingen unlocked him. He was lucky — and even his luck depended on wealthy parents who shielded him from expulsion after the poisoned-apple incident. The wider tragedy is the countless equivalent minds who never reach their Gottingen, because the system is calibrated to the average and punishes those who don't fit.
core_ideas.quote: The tragedy of Oppenheimer is not the Oppenheimer who was, but the many, many countless Oppenheimers who never even were.

core_ideas.explanation: In extraordinary times — wars, existential crises — bureaucracies are forced to recruit mavericks because survival demands creativity (Oppenheimer at 38 leading the Manhattan Project; Ukraine building an Uber for artillery). The mavericks bring with them other mavericks; they look for the clever, not the obedient. But the moment the crisis passes, normal politics reasserts itself, the bureaucracy turns on its own most useful tools, and the McCarthys and Roy Cohns surface to destroy them. This is the rhythm by which societies use and discard their geniuses.
core_ideas.quote: When this kind of Maverick was brought into influence, he would look for the clever ones. He would not look for the obedient ones.

core_ideas.concept: The Renaissance Person vs. The Specialist Silo
core_ideas.explanation: Oppenheimer the experimentalist, theorist, engineer, Sanskrit student, Gita reader, Spanish Civil War sympathiser was the Renaissance man — both fox and hedgehog. Modern academia, driven by journal metrics and narrow funding incentives, forces people into ever-tightening silos until they are 'specializing in something like wheat production in Ukraine between 1836 and 1838.' We have amplified human resources by ten-thousand-fold but we are wasting that firepower because the incentive structure rewards depth-without-breadth.
core_ideas.quote: We've amplified human resources a thousandfold, ten thousandfold, but we're really not getting the kind of commensurate advances that are required.

core_ideas.explanation: A technician knows one narrow skill, executes it, and is not understanding the world or participating in it. An intellectual thinks about the world on a larger scale and connects ideas. Modern institutions produce technicians at scale — credentialed, ladder-climbing, narrowly competent — and starve intellectuals. Edward Teller was a brilliant technician on fusion; Oppenheimer the intellectual was the one who asked whether the world should have a hydrogen bomb at all.
core_ideas.quote: Technicians are people who know one narrow thing... and intellectuals are people who think about the world on a larger scale.

core_ideas.concept: Culture Decides Which Genes Get Expressed
core_ideas.explanation: With seven billion humans alive, the universe is throwing seven billion darts of potential genius. What determines which talents rise are the institutions and culture that do the sorting. A culture that prizes mavericks expresses those genes; a conservative culture obsessed with order and protecting 'the way things have been' expresses dullness. The constraint is not biology — it is institutional selection.
core_ideas.quote: When a culture favors dull people, then that society ends up expressing those genes.

core_ideas.concept: States Can Be Forced to Admit Error
core_ideas.explanation: The defining feature of a first-world country is not that the state never errs — it does, constantly — but that independent citizens can write letters, dig into archives, challenge it in public, and force it to officially own up. The 2022 reinstatement of Oppenheimer's security clearance was that mechanism in action. India does not even expect its state to try.
core_ideas.quote: Being a first world country means being a country where independent people are able to challenge the United States government and get it to the point of officially saying that we were wrong.

core_ideas.concept: Cultures of Cruelty Persist Through Mentorship
core_ideas.explanation: Roy Cohn worked for McCarthy persecuting Oppenheimer in the 1950s; he later mentored Donald Trump. The same nationalist, power-hungry, unethical culture runs as a continuous thread across half a century of American politics through personal lineages. The 'culture war' is not a metaphor — it is one team, with a continuous coaching tree, against another team across generations.
core_ideas.quote: Suddenly you see the threads of history intertwining with each other.

core_ideas.concept: Buildings Shape the People Who Inhabit Them
core_ideas.explanation: Robert Moses' top-down vision of New York — flyovers, bridges, indifference to neighborhoods — did not just produce the city we see today; it produced the people and culture that inhabit that city. The choice between top-down planning and organic growth (Moses vs. Jacobs) is therefore not a technical urban-planning question but a question about who we want to become.
core_ideas.quote: We shape our buildings, and our buildings shape us. — Winston Churchill

core_ideas.explanation: Jane Jacobs' phrase for the spontaneous, organic social life of well-functioning cities — the unplanned choreography of strangers, vendors, children, deliveries that gives urban life its texture. Ajay says he thought of it constantly during COVID lockdowns: the buildings were still there, but the ballet was disrupted, and that disruption is what people actually felt. Indian urban thinking, oscillating between unplanned overgrown villages and authoritarian Chandigarh-style design, urgently needs this middle path.

The 1954 process against Oppenheimer was not justice — it was the illegal extraction of personal information and its release through the machinery of investigation and trial. In today's language: information warfare. Democracies must protect citizens from state-sponsored character assassination, and the rule of law must apply even (especially) to the powerful state.
core_ideas.quote: That was basically character assassination, in today's language we would call it information warfare.

core_ideas.explanation: The Oppenheimer rehabilitation surfaced the children and grandchildren of both the persecutors and the persecuted, carrying institutional memory across generations. India, by contrast, is ahistorical — the people in positions of influence rarely carry that institutional memory, do not know what their predecessors fought over and why, and therefore keep losing battles their forebears already won. Forgetting is a form of disarmament.
core_ideas.quote: We're very ahistorical today. The people we meet in positions of influence very often don't carry this institutional memory.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's name for filmmakers like Christopher Nolan and Denis Villeneuve who bring artistic, intimate, intellectual sensibility into mainstream big-budget cinema — refusing the dichotomy that intimate drama goes to OTT and big spectacle to theatres. They straddle both worlds because the studios trust them enough to let them try new things. The fact that this exists is part of why Amit calls this 'a golden age of world cinema, even if we bemoan the arts.'

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: General Groves on Oppenheimer: 'This is one guy who's good at everything — metallurgy, engineering, chemistry, and of course a genius theoretical physicist. The only thing he can't do is sports.' Amit, deadpan, to Ajay: 'Kinda like you — you know everything except sport. Bollywood perhaps.'

Amit's caricature of academic specialization run amok: a scholar 'specializing in something like wheat production in Ukraine between the years 1836 to 1838.' Funny because it's only barely a caricature.
Ajay challenges Indians who are amazed that Oppenheimer learned Sanskrit: 'For an analogy, I challenge people in India to go learn Aramaic. Okay, we don't do that.'

The Freddie quiz-question gag: Amit's dog Freddie is named after two heroes; Ajay asks, 'Was one of them born in Zanzibar?' Amit: 'None of them was born in Zanzibar, none of them is Freddie Mercury. I'm sorry if that gets the temperature down immediately.'

Ajay on Indian state expectations: 'We in India think that the state is cruel and every now and then the state will crucify many innocent people... but beyond that, we never expect the Indian state to make up and try to admit a mistake.'

'I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.' — the Bhagavad Gita line Oppenheimer recalled at the Trinity test, where Krishna shows his Vishwarup form to Arjun. Iconic to the point of cliche, but earned: Oppenheimer had actually learned Sanskrit and read the Gita.

Ernest Rutherford, on extracting power from atoms: 'Anyone who expects a source of power from these atoms is talking moonshine.' Used here as a case study in how even great minds can fail to see what is invisible until the engineering catches up — Rutherford said this before Szilard's chain-reaction insight.

Sitzfleisch — the German word ('sitting flesh') Murray Gell-Mann used to explain why Oppenheimer never won a Nobel. He had ideas but lacked the patience to sit and grind out the calculations. Wolfgang Pauli said the same thing more bluntly: good at ideas, not at calculation.

Borges' 'On Exactitude in Science' — the fable of cartographers who made a map the same size as the empire. Invoked to describe Caro's obsessive biographical method (he took longer to write about LBJ's Senate years than LBJ spent in the Senate).
Isaiah Berlin's hedgehog and fox — the fox knows many things, the hedgehog knows one big thing. Oppenheimer is the rare creature who is both.

'There are very fine people on both sides' — Trump's Charlottesville line. Ajay quotes it ironically: with the distance of history, the McCarthy/Roy Cohn/Trump tradition versus the Oppenheimer tradition was never a both-sides story.

'Hello, is it me you're looking for?' / 'Hello, can you hear me, I'm in California dreaming about who we used to be' — Amit teases Ajay by pointing out that the closing 'Hello' line he says echoes Lionel Richie's 'Hello' and Adele's 'Hello'.
